clinicalPearls: A granulation-tissue lesion over the vocal process of the arytenoid, where thin mucosa lies directly over cartilage and is prone to trauma
The dominant causes are laryngopharyngeal reflux, phonotrauma with hard glottal attack and throat clearing, and mucosal injury from endotracheal intubation
Presents with throat pain or discomfort, a globus sensation, chronic throat clearing, and mild voice change rather than marked hoarseness
Often unilateral but may be bilateral, forming 'kissing' lesions on the opposing vocal processes
First-line treatment is medical and behavioural, combining antireflux measures with voice therapy to reduce injurious vocal habits
Recurrence after excision alone is high, so surgery is reserved for persistent, enlarging, or airway-threatening lesions or when biopsy is needed
In an intubated or recently extubated patient, tube-related trauma is a common precipitant
reference.pathophysiology: A vocal process granuloma is a benign reparative proliferation of granulation tissue rather than a neoplasm. The mucosa over the arytenoid vocal process is thin and firmly bound to underlying cartilage, so it is readily injured by forceful vocal fold contact, chronic cough or throat clearing, or an endotracheal tube. Once the epithelium is breached and perichondrium exposed, refluxed acid and pepsin reaching the posterior larynx impair healing and sustain inflammation, prompting exuberant granulation tissue to form at the site. Persistence of the causative trauma and reflux explains the strong tendency to recur unless these factors are corrected.
additionalDifferentials: Chondroma or chondrosarcoma of the arytenoid
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to localise the lesion over the vocal process
Videostroboscopy to assess vibration and glottic closure
Speech and language therapy evaluation of hard glottal attack and throat clearing
Biopsy of persistent or atypical lesions to exclude malignancy or specific granulomatous disease
redFlags: Continued enlargement despite adequate reflux and voice treatment
Impaired arytenoid or vocal fold mobility
Airway compromise from a large or bilateral posterior lesion
Systemic features suggesting vasculitis, tuberculosis, or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Resolution with medical and behavioural treatment is the rule but is often slow over several months, and recurrence is common when reflux and phonotrauma persist; overall outcomes are good once the underlying insults are controlled.
pitfalls: Proceeding to repeated excision without controlling reflux and vocal behaviour, perpetuating recurrence
Mislabelling a persistent lesion as benign granuloma without histology to exclude malignancy
Failing to recognise recent intubation as the precipitating trauma
Impatience with the naturally slow resolution, prompting unnecessary surgery
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Antireflux therapy with a proton pump inhibitor plus reflux-precaution lifestyle measures to promote mucosal healing
Voice therapy to eliminate hard glottal attack and habitual throat clearing
Treat any chronic cough contributing to repeated mucosal trauma
Botulinum toxin injection to reduce forceful vocal-process contact in resistant cases
Reserve surgical excision for persistent, enlarging or airway-threatening lesions or diagnostic biopsy, given the high recurrence when the cause is untreated
ENT laryngology and speech therapy referral with monitoring for recurrence
